query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: Chemical short-range ordering (SRO) at grain boundaries in high-entropy nanoalloys lowers grain boundary mobility at high temperatures, thereby slowing grain coarsening and stabilizing the single-phase structure under thermal exposure.
generation.material_initial_state: A quinary W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf nanoalloy (or a similar multi-component system) processed into a nominally single-phase solid solution with limited initial SRO.
generation.intervention: Vary the degree of SRO by pre-annealing selected samples under controlled time–temperature conditions, then compare their evolution during subsequent high-temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Perform in-situ high-temperature TEM and APT from 800–1200 K to measure grain evolution and local compositions over a specified duration similar for all samples.
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range chemical ordering near grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: SRO locally reduces grain-boundary energy and slows boundary migration, limiting both grain growth and compositional segregation during thermal exposure.
generation.predicted_outcome: All else being equal, alloys with higher pre-induced SRO exhibit slower grain growth and retain more uniform composition at boundaries compared to baseline samples lacking such ordering, until temperatures exceed SRO’s critical threshold.
generation.baseline: An equivalent composition processed to minimize SRO via a different pre-annealing schedule or rapid quench, serving as the reference for microstructural evolution rates.
generation.boundary: The stabilizing effect of SRO should vanish above the temperature that destroys short-range order; materials not prone to SRO are expected to show no difference in boundary mobility.
generation.uncertainty: Secondary phase precipitation or concurrent defect interactions (e.g., irradiation damage, solute clustering) could mask or overwhelm SRO’s contribution, complicating direct measurement.

falsification_experiment.design: Expose SRO-enhanced versus SRO-minimized samples to in-situ high-temperature TEM and perform APT at set intervals to track boundary migration and elemental partitioning as a function of annealing time.
measurements: Real-time grain size evolution (via TEM images)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under identical conditions, the putatively high-SRO sample shows the same rate of grain coarsening and chemical segregation as the baseline with minimal SRO, then the hypothesis that SRO significantly retards boundary mobility and stabilizes the microstructure is falsified.

The synthesized quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA shows high thermal stability in terms of grain coarsening. Even though there was an increase in the grain size during He implantation, the material preserved its nano-crystallinity and showed only approximately 10 nm change in grain size after ~8.45 at.% He implantation. The previously studied quaternary W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA demonstrated a similar thermal stability regarding grain morphology [22] . One of the properties that distinguishes this quinary W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf RHEA from the previously studied RHEAs is the grain refinement observed during dual-beam irradiation. Grain refinement was observed before in other materials [32] . Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are designed for high elevated-temperature strength, with both edge and screw dislocations playing an important role for plastic deformation. However, they can also display a significant energetic driving force for chemical short-range ordering (SRO). Here, we investigate mechanisms underlying the mobilities of screw and edge dislocations in the body-centered cubic MoNbTaW RHEA over a wide temperature range using extensive molecular dynamics simulations based on a highly-accurate machine-learning interatomic potential. Further, we specifically evaluate how these mechanisms are affected by the presence of SRO. The mobility of edge dislocations is found to be enhanced by the presence of SRO, whereas the rate of double-kink nucleation in the motion of screw dislocations is reduced, although this influence of SRO appears to be attenuated at increasing temperature. Independent of the presence of SRO, a cross-slip locking mechanism is observed for the motion of screws, which provides for extra strengthening for refractory high-entropy alloy system.

frame.system: High-entropy nanoalloys in a single-phase solid-solution state, intended for elevated-temperature service (e.g., 800–1200 K) with nanoscale features and complex multi-element compositions.
frame.goal: Determine the key mechanistic factors that govern the structural and chemical stability of high-entropy nanoalloys when exposed to high temperatures.
frame.limitation: Unclear how entropic stabilization, local chemical ordering, and interfacial energies jointly control phase stability and microstructural evolution at the nanoscale under thermal stress.

prior_attempts: Standard thermodynamic and phase-diagram approaches have been used at bulk scales, but they often do not fully explain behavior at the nano-regime. decision.trend: Early work on W-based refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) with nanocrystalline or ultrafine grains (PMC6397024, 2019) showed promising stability under high-temperature irradiation, implying that local composition and nanoscale precipitation can reduce defect formation. Subsequent atomistic simulations (PMC8357793, 2021) demonstrated that short-range chemical ordering in single-phase MoNbTaW can significantly modify dislocation mobility and hence affects high-temperature mechanical behavior. Most recently, experiments on a quinary W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf nanoalloy (PMC10154406, 2023) revealed stable nanoscale grains up to ~1173 K without significant loss of structural integrity, indicating that subtle interactions among elemental partitioning, grain boundaries, and local ordering stabilize the alloy at elevated temperatures.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear how entropic stabilization, local chemical short-range order (SRO), and interfacial energies collectively govern the long-term phase stability and microstructural evolution of these nanoscale RHEAs under prolonged high-temperature exposure (800–1200 K). The precise mechanisms by which SRO and interface chemistry slow grain growth, stabilize single-phase solid solutions, or alter diffusion pathways have yet to be experimentally isolated and verified.
decision.lever: Perform an in-situ high-temperature TEM/APT study comparing samples with different pre-annealing treatments that alter the degree of short-range chemical order, then track grain evolution and local compositions during annealing at 800–1200 K over time.
decision.why: A direct microstructural comparison under controlled SRO conditions will test the hypothesis that chemical short-range ordering at grain boundaries reduces interface mobility and enhances nanoscale stability. Relative to a baseline material with lower SRO, the high-SRO sample is predicted to show slower grain coarsening and more stable local chemistry under thermal exposure. This effect should vanish if temperatures exceed the SRO critical temperature or if compositional gradients do not form. If, under appropriately controlled conditions, both sets of samples exhibit indistinguishable coarsening rates and chemical evolution, it would falsify the proposed mechanistic role of SRO in stabilizing nanoscale grains at high temperatures.
